title: Loops over data, and the first cow story
summary: Teach Python to read a whole file and answer questions about it, then plan a real farm problem on paper and send it to the grader that judges everybody.
materials: laptop with Python and the editor installed in week 1
your Season 2 robot-data folder, with lamp_on.txt still in it
paper and pencil for drawing the farm
a parent-created USACO account for past problems
a grown-up free for twenty minutes to belay at the keyboard

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop first: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: last week your program listened to a few lines you typed in yourself. What happens when the question arrives a hundred lines long, or a thousand? Nobody types a thousand lines by hand, and nobody wants to read a thousand lines to find the biggest one.

Imagine: a loop that visits every line exactly once, carrying one small answer in its hand and updating it as it goes. To count, the hand starts at 0 and goes up by one at every line. To add up, the hand starts at 0 and grows by whatever the line says. To find the biggest, the hand starts holding the first number and swaps only when a bigger one walks past. Three different questions, one shape underneath: visit each one once, keep a running answer. That shape is the one you will use all season, and it is the same shape the shop's cost sheet will need in a few weeks.

Plan, part one: point that loop at your own data. Season 2 left you a folder called robot-data holding lamp_on.txt, lamp_off.txt, hand_near.txt and hand_far.txt, ten readings each, one number per line, every one of them measured off the robot by you. Copy lamp_on.txt into the season folder git has been watching since week 1, so this week's program and its save points live in the same place. Then make Python tell you how many readings are in that file, what they add up to, and which one was the highest.

Plan, part two: the farm. Farmer John has a milk problem, and it is a real past USACO Bronze problem called Mixing Milk that thousands of people have solved. A grown-up finds it from the past contests list on the USACO site, under the Bronze problems, and opens the problem page for you. Today it is a story before it is anything else. You read it aloud, you draw the buckets on paper, and you move the milk with a pencil until you can say what happens without guessing. Only then does anyone open the editor.

Plan, part three: the grader. When the program works on the sample, it goes to the real USACO grader, the same one that judges everybody. This one is a paired climb. The plan is yours and every decision is yours; a grown-up sits at the keyboard and drives while you call the moves, the way a belayer holds the rope while the climber picks the route. The verdict belongs to you either way, and it does not know or care how old you are.

One last thing, about save points. Last week git started keeping camps along your trail. This week the message on each camp starts doing real work. A message that says what changed is a message the computer could have written by itself: it can already see that three lines moved. A message that says why is the one future you will need. Compare fixed readings.py with skipped the blank last line, which was crashing int() before the file finished. Only one of those two is worth reading in a month. Write why.

Five minutes of typing, hands on the home row, eyes on the screen. Today's words are the ones this week's code needs: open, for, in, line, strip, int, total, count, print, commit. Type each word five times. Then type the line for line in open('lamp_on.txt'): three times without looking at your fingers, and land the colon at the end every single time.

steps.title: Point a loop at your own data
steps.body:
Copy lamp_on.txt out of your Season 2 robot-data folder into the season folder you made in week 1, the one git is watching. Then open the editor and start a new file called readings.py, saved in that same folder, beside the copy.

Type this program:

total = 0
count = 0
biggest = None
for line in open('lamp_on.txt'):
    line = line.strip()
    if line == '':
        continue
    n = int(line)
    total = total + n
    count = count + 1
    if biggest is None or n > biggest:
        biggest = n

print('readings', count)
print('total', total)
print('biggest', biggest)

Read it out loud before you run it, one line at a time, saying what each hand is holding at that moment. The three variables at the top are three hands: one holds a running total, one holds a running count, one holds the biggest seen so far. The loop visits each line once and updates the hands. The three prints sit outside the loop on purpose, because an answer announced before every line has been visited is not an answer, it is a guess.

Now check it without trusting it. Copy the first five lines of lamp_on.txt into a new file called five.txt, then add those five readings up by hand on paper. Change the file name inside readings.py to five.txt, run it, and compare. If your paper and the program disagree, one of you is wrong, and finding out which one is the entire job. Put the name back to lamp_on.txt when you are done.

Then commit. Use git add on readings.py, then git commit with a message that says why this file exists, not what you typed. Change one thing, run it again, and commit again with a message that says why you changed it.
checklist: readings.py prints a count, a total and a biggest, and I said out loud what each hand was holding
I added the first five readings by hand and the program agreed with my paper
My loop visits every line exactly once, and nothing prints until the loop is finished
Both commit messages say why, and a grown-up could not have guessed either one just by looking at the changed lines

steps.title: What a judge server does with your file
steps.body:
When you press submit, your .py file leaves your laptop and lands on a computer that has never met you. Here is what that computer does with it.

It puts your file in a small sealed room where it cannot touch anything else on the machine. It feeds your program an input you have never seen, one of a set of secret test cases, and it starts a stopwatch. Your program runs, prints its answer and stops. The server compares what you printed against what the answer should be, character by character. Not nearly. A missing space, a capital letter where a small one belonged, or an extra blank line at the end can be the whole difference between accepted and not.

Then it does the same thing with the next test case, and the next, watching the stopwatch every time. If your program is still thinking when the time limit runs out, that test fails even though your answer would have been right eventually. That is why counting the steps before you run one matters, and you will meet that idea properly later in the season.

The server does not know your name, your age or how long you worked. It reads a file and a clock. That is exactly what makes its verdict worth having.

figure.alt: A bat shouts near 200,000 hertz and listens for the echo. Sound travels about 343 metres a second, so the delay before the echo returns tells the bat how far the moth is; its large folded ears funnel the faint echo back like a dish antenna.

steps.title: A bat runs your sensor's trick, only better
steps.body:
Last season your ultrasonic sensor found distance by timing an echo. A bat has run the same trick its whole life, and it is far better at it than your robot was.

A bat shouts, mostly in tones far above human hearing, some calls near 200,000 hertz, then listens for the return. Sound moves at about 343 metres a second in air. The delay before the echo tells the bat exactly how far away the moth is.

Its ears are shaped to help: large, often oddly folded flaps funnel a faint echo into the ear canal. It is the animal's own dish antenna. Some bats can even judge a moth's texture and wingbeat from tiny changes in the returning echo.

Your lamp_on.txt and lamp_off.txt held ten readings each. A hunting bat effectively reruns its own version of that experiment dozens of times a second, correcting course after every echo.

figure.alt: Buckets sit in a row, each with a size and current amount from the problem page. Milk pours from one bucket to the next in order; each pour moves whichever is smaller, the room left in the receiver or the milk in the giver, and stops the moment one hits its limit.

steps.title: The first cow story, and the real grader
steps.body:
Open the Mixing Milk problem page and read the problem out loud. All of it, including the boring part about where the input comes from and where the answer goes, in a normal voice, to an actual person. If you cannot read a sentence out loud without stumbling, you have not understood it yet.

Then close the laptop and draw the farm. Buckets as rectangles on paper, each bucket's size written on the side and how much milk is in it right now written inside. In this story milk is poured from one bucket into the next, over and over in a set order, and every pour stops the moment the giving bucket runs empty or the receiving bucket runs full. How many buckets there are, how big they are, how much milk each starts with and how many pours happen are all written in the problem itself, not in this plan. Copy those numbers onto your drawing.

Now move the milk with a pencil. Do the first three pours by hand, crossing out old amounts and writing the new ones beside them. This is the exact move from this week's warm-up: work out the room left in the receiving bucket, compare it with what the giving bucket is holding, and the smaller of those two is what moves. Three pours by hand is enough to know the rule in your fingers.

Write the plan on paper before any code. Three lines is plenty: what the program reads, what it does over and over, what it prints at the end. Then say out loud how many pours the loop will do, and why that number is small enough for a laptop to finish before you blink.

Now the paired climb. A grown-up sits at the keyboard. You call every move: which variable, which line, what belongs inside the loop. They type exactly what you say, including your mistakes, because your mistakes are the interesting part of the hour. When the program runs on the sample from the problem page and matches the sample answer exactly, you submit it to the real USACO grader.

Before you submit, read the problem page's input and output instructions one more time and follow them to the letter. A correct program that puts its answer in the wrong place is still rejected, and that is the most common way a good solution fails.

Then read the verdict together. If it is accepted, that is the real grader accepting your code. If it is not, write down exactly which test failed and what the message said, and try one honest fix. A rejection you can explain is worth more than an acceptance you cannot.
checklist: I read the whole problem out loud to a person before anything was opened
The farm is drawn on paper with every bucket's size and starting milk written on it
I moved the milk by hand for the first three pours before a line of code was typed
I called every move while a grown-up typed, and the program matched the sample answer exactly before we submitted
The verdict, accepted or not, is written down in my own words

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body: One line for each thing that did not work the first time, and what you tried. The classics this week: a file opened under the wrong name, so Python says it cannot find it; a blank last line in lamp_on.txt reaching int() and crashing the program; a print left inside the loop, so you get one answer per line instead of one answer; biggest starting at 0 when it should start empty, so a file of readings below zero reports 0 forever; and an answer that is right but printed in a shape the grader will not take. Write down which one caught you, or the brand new one you found, and what fixed it.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of your paper farm with the milk moved by hand, the Python for both programs pasted or as a share link, and a photo of the grader's verdict screen, whatever it says.
